reason: The cited evidence (E1) supports that increased dislocation density and grain boundary density promote thicker, less defective passivation films and provide more nucleation sites, but it refers to a different alloy (CR75) and attributes passivation to ultrafine grain size, not solely dislocation density. The hypothesis overstates the direct applicability to Q235 steel and assumes dislocation density can be isolated from grain size effects, which E1 does not confirm.
premises: High dislocation density promotes uniform, adherent Fe-oxide passive film on Q235 steel
Increased dislocation density provides more active nucleation sites for oxidation
Low dislocation density leads to heterogeneous, less protective oxide film
Grain size can be kept constant while varying dislocation density via annealing
Dislocation density is the dominant factor governing protective oxide formation and corrosion suppression
